html:
The largest public baths of ancient Rome, built from 298 to 306 and named after the emperor Diocletian. Maximian began the work after a visit to the city, and it was finished after both men had retired.

The complex covered about 13 hectares on the high ground near today's Termini station and could serve some 3,000 bathers at once, about twice as many as the Baths of Caracalla. Like other great baths it had cold, warm and hot halls, a swimming pool, exercise yards, and space for reading and talk.

It was used until the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537. In the 1560s Michelangelo turned the great vaulted hall into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli, and the ancient vaults still stand above it. Other parts hold the National Roman Museum.
sum: The largest public baths of ancient Rome, built from 298 to 306 and named after the emperor Diocletian. Maximian began the work after a visit to the city, and it was finished after both men had retired.
